title: David's Repentance and Flight
english: …is found to have befallen him, yet he showed that the falls of the saints are quickly set right.
“And David said to Nathan, ‘I have sinned against the Lord’” (2 Samuel 12:13). (Cyril, from his exposition of Psalm 51.) Here, I ask you, marvel at the blessed David: … he mourned over his sin.

“Moreover, the son born to you shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:14). (Cyril, from his Commentary on the Psalter, on the verse “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger” (Psalm 6:1 or Psalm 38:1).) And yet, having heard these things from the prophet, … rather than to be pardoned.

“And he took the crown of Molchom the king” (2 Samuel 12:30). He set himself in battle against the sons of Ammon and against those who had joined shields with them in their madness, I mean those from the land of the Syrians. He conquered and took them by force; and taking the crown of Molchom, and finding in it a very large and precious stone, he bound it onto his own crown.

“And David went up weeping, with his head covered” (2 Samuel 15:30). Since it happened that before the war against Absalom the blessed David had committed the sin, I mean the one against Uriah, there was talk throughout the whole land of the Jews, so to speak, and some held a not unlikely suspicion about him. For they thought that he was paying the penalty for his offenses against Uriah, and that, since he had offended God, he would now be easy prey for any who wished and weak on every side. “Scatter, I beg you, the counsel…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, continuing the last sentence of the previous section.
Two '...' marks in the copy-text are the compiler's cuts; they are kept as ellipses and nothing is supplied.

Sigla naming other works are kept as short parentheses: 'ἐκ τῆς εἰς τὸν νʹ ψαλμόν' (LXX Psalm 50, given in English numbering as Psalm 51) and 'ἐκ τοῦ εἰς ψαλτήριον ὑπομνήματος, ῥητοῦ προκειμένου' (Commentary on the Psalter, on the verse set out). Plain '{Κυρίλλου.}' sigla are not rendered.
Context suggests the 'Lord, do not rebuke me' psalm is Psalm 38 (LXX 37), a penitential psalm, but Psalm 6 opens with the same words; both are given.
'Molchom' kept as Cyril spells it (LXX Μολχολ; Hebrew malkam, 'their king', or Milcom).
'νοσοῦντα τὸ ἄναλκι' rendered 'weak on every side' with πανταχοῦ.
The column number 69.685 is not rendered. The closing lemma breaks off at the section boundary and continues in the next section.

title: Ahithophel, Hushai, and Shimei
english: …of Ahithophel” (2 Samuel 15:31). “Scatter,” he says, “the counsel of Ahithophel, O Lord my God.” For Ahithophel was deep, bitter and full of schemes, able to find a way in every matter, and on top of this a most skilled general. So David feared Ahithophel most of all, because he always put forward bitter counsels and knew how to command an army.

“And behold, Hushai came to meet him” (2 Samuel 15:32). He persuades Hushai, who was one of his own friends, to feign desertion from him and a wish to be taken into Absalom’s service, so that he might secretly fight against the counsels of Ahithophel; and that is just what happened.

“And thus Shimei said as he cursed him” (2 Samuel 16:7). Though Shimei insulted him and all but hurled bitter words at him as from a sling, he went away having suffered nothing from David at that time, even though afterward he paid a harsh penalty that he deserved (1 Kings 2:44–46). The point is that David endured, and though many urged him on, he counted silence worth everything, out of very great and admirable understanding.

For he reasoned that, because he had offended God, he had in some way been given over to scourges, and he counted the reproaches, taunts and laughter of certain people as part of the blow. For where there is turning away and abandonment by God, even if it falls on someone only in moderate degree, there, without doubt, will be many bitter things of the kind that bring deep grief.
translator_notes: Opens by completing the lemma split at the end of the previous section. Plain '{Κυρίλλου.}' sigla and the page number '2' are not rendered.
'David' is supplied for the subject of 'feared' and for 'him' after Shimei where the Greek uses only the verb or a pronoun; no content is added.

'προσποιήσασθαι' governs both infinitives: Hushai is to feign both the desertion and the wish to join Absalom ('τὸ προσκεκλῆσθαι θέλειν τὸν Ἀβεσσαλὼμ', rendered by sense 'a wish to be taken into Absalom’s service').
'κατασφενδονήσας' (to sling down at) rendered 'hurled bitter words at him as from a sling', echoing the stones of 2 Samuel 16:6.
'παρατρυνόντων' read as παροτρυνόντων, 'urging on'; Abishai's urging (2 Samuel 16:9) may lie behind 'many', not cited inline since Cyril speaks generally.
'καταλυπεῖν' taken as 'grieve sorely' (not καταλιπεῖν, 'leave behind'), hence 'the kind that bring deep grief'.
baehrens: PG 69; Fragmenta in Regum b02 rem mid

title: Ahithophel's End and Absalom's Death
english: “Because the Lord told him to curse David” (2 Samuel 16:10). He recalls this in Psalm 39, where he says: “You have made me a reproach to the fool” (Psalm 39:8).

“And Ahithophel said to Absalom,” and so on (2 Samuel 17:1). Absalom wanted to pursue his father as he fled, and Ahithophel boldly advised that this must be done. But Hushai, persuasively drawing him back, urged him to keep in view his father’s fierceness, and not simply to rush straight at the task, but rather first to make ready a sufficient force and gather a crowd of soldiers, because the blessed David was mighty, skilled in war, and among the most warlike of all.

“And the woman took and spread the covering,” and so on (2 Samuel 17:19). So then, even if at times good things come to us through men, let us not give thanks to them rather than to God, who through them has granted us what gladdens the heart.

“And Ahithophel saw that his counsel had not been followed” (2 Samuel 17:23). The opinion of Hushai prevailed; and Ahithophel, deeply grieved at this, ended his life with a noose, bringing a just sentence against himself.

“And he wept, and thus he said,” and so on (2 Samuel 18:33). Absalom made war on the blessed David, and the young man unexpectedly took up the weapons of hostility against the one who begot him; but he was caught and perished. Yet his father did not rejoice over him when he met his death, but mourned him as a son.
translator_notes: Plain '{Κυρίλλου.}' sigla and the column number 69.688 are not rendered.
Psalm numbering converted: 'ληʹ' (LXX 38) is Psalm 39 in English Bibles; the verse is LXX 38:9 = Psalm 39:8.

In 'ἀφιστὰς τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς ἀγριότητος ἐπιδεῖν' the verb of advising is implied from the preceding clause; 'urged him' is supplied so the infinitives read as Hushai's advice (compare 2 Samuel 17:7–13).
